subtitle: Base performance review judgments on clear expectations and relevant evidence, not on familiarity or assumptions. You will also learn to follow up constructively after the review.
scope: For DHS supervisors conducting or preparing performance conversations. Follow current agency procedures, applicable bargaining agreements and HR guidance for actual reviews, records and employment actions. This course is a learning aid, not a new rating system or an investigation process. Never place real personnel records, medical information or inferred IDI orientations in course responses.
introTranscript: Fair performance review is an ongoing responsibility, not a search for the right adjective at the end of a year. Employees need understandable expectations, useful feedback and a review grounded in the work they actually had the opportunity to perform. Bias-aware review asks whether familiarity, visibility, recent events or communication style are replacing evidence. It does not require diagnosing a supervisor’s motives or avoiding difficult feedback. Across six lessons you will clarify expectations, examine evidence, improve review language, compare judgments responsibly, hold a constructive conversation and review the process. The practice activities help leaders practice; actual employment decisions remain in their responsible channels.

lessons.title: Make expectations clear before the review
lessons.summary: Define the work result and relevant standards rather than relying on unwritten preferences.
lessons.objective: Rewrite a vague expectation as an observable work requirement.
objectives: Rewrite a vague expectation as an observable work requirement.
Explain how an expectation relates to a role’s purpose.
Identify a change that needs responsible review rather than retrospective application.
takeaways: Explain what a useful result looks like.
Do not introduce hidden standards at review time.
lessons.statement: An employee should be able to understand the standard before being judged against it.

image.caption: A fair review begins with an understandable expectation.

intro.heading: Clarify the requirement and its purpose
intro.body:
A review can become a debate about personality when expectations were never made clear. A supervisor may ask for professionalism, initiative or collaboration without explaining what those terms mean for the role. At review time, the employee learns that the supervisor expected a particular communication style, meeting habit or level of visibility. Bias-aware review begins earlier by connecting expectations to actual responsibilities and observable work.

Choose one expectation and explain its purpose. If the employee prepares recommendations, the work may need a clear decision question, appropriate evidence and an accurate account of uncertainty. If the role coordinates a process, the expectation may involve timely communication of a delay and its next step. These descriptions make the result visible without requiring the employee to resemble the supervisor.

Distinguish necessary conduct and results from preferences. Respectful communication and accurate work can be real requirements. A preference for spontaneous verbal updates instead of a useful written update may not be the same kind of requirement. Examine the role’s needs and current procedures before judging an unfamiliar style. Do not remove legitimate standards merely because feedback could feel uncomfortable.

Explain expectations and invite questions while there is time to act. Ask the employee to describe the next task and the point where a decision or support is needed. This can reveal an instruction gap. If duties or conditions change, use the responsible process to clarify the new expectations; do not quietly apply a new standard backward to completed work.

Actual performance plans and rating procedures follow agency and applicable employment requirements. This exercise does not create a substitute system or authorize an informal employment rule. It offers a way to make the basis of a review understandable, so feedback can address the work rather than a hidden picture of the ideal employee.

lessons.keyStatement: A useful standard tells the employee what the work requires and why it matters.

flashcards.back: A work result or conduct requirement explained through the applicable supervisory process.
Relevant information about what was done, under what conditions and with what result.
A judgment using an indirect feature, such as visibility or familiarity, instead of examining the required work.
A responsible comparison of how standards and evidence are interpreted; it is not a popularity vote.
A specific account of a work feature, its effect and a practical next step.

items.title: “Show more initiative”
items.body: Describe the initiative the work requires, such as raising a foreseeable risk and proposing an appropriate next action. Explain authority boundaries as well. An employee should not have to choose between guessing a hidden expectation and acting beyond their role to appear ambitious.

items.title: “Communicate professionally”
items.body: Connect the expectation to accuracy, respect and the reader’s ability to use the information. Avoid treating accent, eye contact or similarity to the supervisor as the standard without a work-related basis. Formal conduct requirements remain in effect; the course does not excuse disrespect or inaccurate communication.

items.title: “Be collaborative”
items.body: Explain what cooperation looks like in the task: sharing relevant drafts, responding to dependencies or raising disagreements respectfully. A person can collaborate without attending every optional gathering or speaking most often. The expectation should distinguish reliable work behavior from a preferred social style.

tabs.label: Purpose
tabs.body: Purpose connects an expectation to the role and the people who depend on the result. “Show initiative” can mean several different things unless the work action is explained. Describe the responsibility, such as raising a blocked dependency before a deadline. This makes the expectation more useful than an impression about how an employee should appear.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence describes what would demonstrate the result or conduct, with relevant context. A supervisor can assess whether the employee identified a risk and communicated it through the agreed route. They cannot fairly invent that expectation only after the task is complete. Clear evidence helps distinguish a genuine work requirement from a preference for a familiar style.

tabs.label: Communication
tabs.body: Communication makes the expectation understandable through the responsible process. Invite questions about examples, review points and changing conditions. If a standard needs revision, explain it prospectively with any required HR guidance. A performance conversation should examine an expectation the employee could use, rather than announcing hidden rules as though they had always been obvious.

check.question: A review draft says an employee lacks initiative but provides no expectation or example. What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Identify the work-related expectation, relevant examples and whether it was explained before making a review judgment.
wrong: Keep the phrase because supervisors can recognize initiative intuitively.
Replace it with a guess about the employee’s cultural background.
Introduce a new standard and apply it backward to completed work.
check.feedbackCorrect: This checks the basis and fairness of the judgment before turning a vague impression into a review statement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Intuition can identify a question but cannot supply an unexplained work standard. A cultural-background guess replaces evidence with a stereotype. Applying a newly introduced criterion backward prevents the employee from using it when the work was done. Examine the actual expectation, its communication and relevant examples before making a formal judgment.

items.text: Raise a likely deadline delay with the affected colleague and propose a next step.
Have the right executive presence.
Use the same accent and style as the supervisor.
Distinguish confirmed findings from open questions in the briefing.
Be a better cultural fit.
Attend optional social gatherings to prove commitment.

lessons.next: Next, gather a balanced view of work across the relevant period.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Mara drafts a review saying that Cedric needs more initiative. She has not explained what action she expected, and Cedric has raised several documented service risks through the agreed route.
options: The actual expectation, communication of it and relevant work examples before revising the review.
How often Cedric attended voluntary lunch events.
responses: This connects the judgment to a clear standard and work evidence.
Similarity is not the required performance result.
Voluntary social attendance is not a substitute for examining the role’s work.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite two vague review phrases as work expectations with purpose, observable evidence and an authority boundary. Use practice details.

move.control: You can clarify the standard and explain its work connection through responsible supervisory procedures.
move.failure: The review judges a person against preferences that were never made visible.
move.next: Before the next review conversation, check whether every significant expectation has an understandable work basis.

lessons.title: Gather evidence across the period and the work
lessons.summary: Examine relevant examples and conditions rather than allowing the latest event or most visible task to dominate.
lessons.objective: Identify evidence that covers the relevant review period and responsibilities.
objectives: Identify evidence that covers the relevant review period and responsibilities.
Separate an observed work feature from an explanation that is not established.
Identify a condition or support question that affects interpretation.
takeaways: The latest event is not the entire period.
Visible work is not the only contribution.
Context helps interpret evidence without erasing standards.
lessons.statement: Review the work the employee performed, including the conditions and opportunities that shaped it.

image.caption: A balanced review uses relevant examples across the work and period.

intro.heading: Build a view broader than the last impression
intro.body:
A recent success or mistake is easy to remember. A high-profile presentation may be more visible than months of accurate coordination. If those impressions dominate a review, the judgment may not describe the relevant period or the role’s full responsibilities. Gather appropriate work evidence over time and explain what each example shows. Actual documentation must follow current agency procedures; course practice uses invented information.

Identify the responsibilities being reviewed and the applicable period. Consider examples of products, decisions, coordination and conduct relevant to those responsibilities. Do not collect every possible piece of information or monitor private activity. A useful evidence record is proportionate to the work question and kept in approved channels.

Separate observation from interpretation. “The draft omitted the decision owner” is an observation. “The employee does not care about accountability” is an explanation of motive that the observation does not establish. Ask what instruction, access and review were available, and whether the employee had a chance to respond. Context can explain a process gap without automatically excusing a real performance issue.

Examine opportunity and dependency. An employee cannot demonstrate a task they were never assigned or complete a product that depends on unavailable authorized access without a workable alternative. Another employee may have received extra support or a more visible role. These conditions are relevant to interpreting the evidence. They do not justify inventing a rating or ignoring current review requirements; seek HR guidance when needed.

Look for missing evidence as well as contrary evidence. A supervisor’s lack of observation is not proof that no contribution occurred. Ask for relevant work examples through the responsible process and consider evidence that challenges the initial impression. Keep private medical details, inferred cultural orientations and irrelevant personal circumstances out of the learning activity and informal judgment.

inThisLesson: Look for missing and contrary evidence.
lessons.keyStatement: An evidence gap is a reason to examine further, not an automatic negative judgment.

items.title: The most recent event dominates
items.body: A recent event may be important, but explain how it relates to the whole period and standard. Check earlier examples and the seriousness of the event through responsible procedures. Do not simply average everything or disregard a material concern; use a reasoned account of the actual work.

items.title: Only presentations count
items.body: Research, coordination and follow-through can be essential even when someone else presents the result. Identify the employee’s actual contribution and its relevance. Visibility should not become an unexplained substitute for capability or quality. Keep credit accurate in shared work.

items.title: A missing opportunity looks like weak capability
items.body: If an employee never had the relevant assignment, the review cannot treat absence of its product as proof of inability. Examine the role expectation and opportunity provided. Formal assessment and employment questions need responsible guidance rather than an improvised hidden potential label.

tabs.label: Observation
tabs.body: Observation names what the work or action establishes. A missed deadline is an event; “unreliable” is a broader interpretation requiring more evidence. Describe the actual output, timing and response. Keeping those separate allows the employee and supervisor to examine the same facts instead of debating a personality label that the example may not support.

tabs.label: Context
tabs.body: Context includes relevant instructions, access, dependencies and support. If required access was unavailable, examine what alternatives and responses were possible before interpreting the delay. Context does not automatically remove responsibility, but ignoring it can assign a process failure entirely to a person. Keep inquiry focused on the task rather than unnecessary medical or identity information.

tabs.label: Limit
tabs.body: A limit explains what the example cannot establish and what additional evidence is appropriate. One recent event may be memorable without representing the whole review period. Examine evidence across the actual work and avoid speculation about motives or culture. Proportionate collection supports sound judgment; broad private-information gathering does not repair a narrow evidence gap.

check.question: An employee missed a product deadline after required access was unavailable, but the review draft calls them unreliable. What should the supervisor examine?
check.correct: The actual deadline evidence, access dependency, available alternatives and employee response before drawing a broader conclusion.
wrong: Ignore the access issue because context never matters.
Assume one event proves every part of the employee’s performance.
Collect private medical information to explain the delay.
check.feedbackCorrect: This examines the event and relevant conditions without using one impression or unnecessary personal information as the explanation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Ignoring access removes a potentially important dependency. One event cannot automatically establish every aspect of performance. Private medical collection is not a substitute for examining the task and appropriate support process. Consider the deadline, available alternatives and actual employee response, stating what the evidence does and does not establish.

items.text: The briefing omitted the identified decision owner.
The employee did not receive the authorized access required for the task.
The omission proves the employee does not care.
The review product was submitted on the agreed date.
A dependency changed after the work plan was agreed.
Quiet meeting participation proves no contribution occurred.

lessons.next: Next, improve review wording so it describes the work accurately.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leon remembers a recent missed briefing and drafts a low assessment of Naomi’s reliability. Earlier products were timely, and the missed briefing depended on a system approval Naomi had raised before the deadline.
scenario.prompt: What is the sound next step?
options: Use the recent event as the whole review because it is memorable.
Examine relevant examples across the period, the access dependency and the applicable standard before making the assessment.
Remove every performance expectation because access was delayed once.
responses: A memorable event does not necessarily represent the full work or its context.
This creates a balanced and relevant basis while preserving the actual standard and responsible process.
Context should inform interpretation, not automatically erase all standards.

lessons.transfer: Create a sample evidence table with responsibility, example, period, relevant condition and limit. Include one example that challenges an initial impression.

move.control: You can seek appropriate work evidence, review context and avoid unsupported motive claims.
move.failure: A single visible event becomes a permanent judgment while contrary evidence and dependencies are ignored.
move.next: Check the period, work coverage and evidence gaps in the next review draft.

lessons.title: Write feedback about the work rather than the person
lessons.summary: Replace broad labels with specific observations, effects and practical revisions.
lessons.objective: Rewrite a personality-based review phrase using relevant work evidence.
objectives: Rewrite a personality-based review phrase using relevant work evidence.
Explain the effect of an observed feature on the task or service.
Identify language that treats an unfamiliar communication style as a defect without a work basis.
takeaways: Explain its effect on the result.
lessons.statement: A useful review sentence can be acted on without guessing what kind of person the supervisor wants.

image.caption: Specific wording makes feedback clearer and easier to use.

intro.heading: Make the sentence do useful work
intro.body:
Review language can sound polished while remaining vague. Words such as abrasive, passive, confident or polished may describe an impression without identifying the action that affected the work. They can also carry different expectations for employees with different identities or communication styles. Bias-aware writing does not ban every adjective; it asks whether the judgment has a clear, relevant and consistently applied basis.

Begin with an observation. What did the employee say, do, produce or omit? Explain the effect on the reader, decision, colleague or service. Then name a practical next step. “The recommendation did not distinguish the proposed change from the current rule, so readers could not identify the decision; the next draft should separate those sections” is more usable than “be more polished.”

For conduct concerns, describe the relevant behavior and expectation accurately. Respectful communication is a real responsibility; this course does not excuse harmful conduct by calling it a cultural difference. At the same time, an unfamiliar accent, quieter participation or different eye-contact practice is not by itself evidence of disrespect or poor capability. Ask what the work requires and seek responsible guidance on formal concerns.

Check comparative wording. Would the same action be described differently for another employee? Is one person called decisive while another is called difficult for a similar supported challenge? Examine the actual words, context and effect rather than assuming every difference in description proves bias. The purpose is a consistent evidentiary standard, not a diagnosis of the writer’s motive.

Keep the sentence within its evidence. Avoid claims about an employee’s culture, loyalty or intercultural orientation. Do not include private information unnecessary to the work judgment. Actual review records follow approved processes. In this activity, use practice text and practice turning an impression into a specific, defensible and actionable account.

lessons.keyStatement: Clear feedback links evidence, effect and an action rather than assigning a broad personal label.

items.title: “Needs executive presence”
items.body: Ask what useful result the phrase is supposed to describe. If the issue is a briefing that lacks a clear recommendation, say that and explain the reader’s need. Do not use presence as an undefined proxy for accent, confidence, appearance or resemblance to senior colleagues.

items.title: “Is too quiet to collaborate”
items.body: Examine relevant cooperation evidence, such as sharing drafts, responding to dependencies and raising questions appropriately. Meeting volume alone may not show collaboration. If spoken participation is necessary for a particular task, explain that specific requirement and appropriate support rather than assigning a personality defect.

items.title: “Is difficult when challenged”
items.body: Describe the actual response and effect. A respectful disagreement may improve a decision; a harmful interaction may require formal attention. Do not collapse both into one label. Use current conduct expectations and responsible routes for actual concerns while making the work evidence clear.

tabs.label: Feature
tabs.body: A feature is a supported part of the product or interaction. “The brief gives a recommendation without the comparison rationale” is examinable; “be polished” may leave the employee guessing. Start with the feature and avoid attributing an internal motive. That gives both people a clear place to discuss whether the feedback fits the work.

tabs.label: Effect
tabs.body: Effect explains why the feature matters to a reader, decision or service. A missing rationale may prevent a reader from weighing alternatives even when the facts are correct. State that connection rather than asking the employee to imitate the supervisor’s wording. Useful feedback teaches the reason for a standard, not merely the style preferred by one person.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: Action identifies a practical revision and the support or review needed. Adding the comparison and checking whether the reader can follow it makes the feedback usable. An inferred developmental label supplies no work instruction. Keep formal matters in their own route, including applicable immediate reporting duties when a protected-class harassment or discrimination concern arises.

check.question: Which revision makes “be more polished” useful?
check.correct: Identify the specific clarity or accuracy issue, its effect on the intended reader and a practical revision for the next product.
wrong: Tell the employee to imitate the supervisor’s speaking style.
Add more complimentary adjectives without explaining the work.
Assign an inferred intercultural orientation to explain the issue.
check.feedbackCorrect: This makes the feedback actionable and keeps it tied to relevant evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Imitating a supervisor’s speaking style may leave the clarity or accuracy issue unchanged. More complimentary adjectives remain vague. An inferred intercultural orientation is neither a justified personal assessment nor a usable revision instruction. Name the actual product feature, explain its effect and agree on a relevant next action.

items.text: Separate current policy from the proposal so the reader can identify the change.
Develop a better presence.
The employee’s accent shows weak analytical ability.
Name the unresolved question before the recommendation is forwarded.
Be less difficult without any example or effect.
A course attendance pattern reveals the employee’s IDI orientation.

lessons.next: Next, compare judgments responsibly before finalizing a review.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Rhea writes that Tomas is too quiet to collaborate. Tomas consistently shares drafts and resolves dependencies, but speaks less during large meetings. Rhea cannot identify a task that required more speech or an unmet coordination expectation.
options: Keep the label because collaboration should look the same for everyone.
Review the actual cooperation evidence and name a specific work requirement only if the evidence supports it.
responses: Uniform style is not necessarily the role’s required result.
A cultural judgment is not a supported work finding.
This keeps the review tied to the work and avoids converting an unfamiliar style into a defect.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite three practice review phrases using observation, effect and next step. Mark any phrase whose evidence is insufficient for a conclusion.

move.control: You can revise vague language and explain the actual work requirement without diagnosing a person.
move.failure: The employee receives polished labels but no usable account of what to improve.
move.next: Before finalizing a review draft, check whether each significant judgment has evidence, effect and an action.

lessons.title: Compare judgments without turning review into a vote
lessons.summary: Use responsible calibration to examine standards and evidence, not status, popularity or identity.
lessons.objective: Explain a review judgment through its standard and evidence.
objectives: Explain a review judgment through its standard and evidence.
Identify a calibration discussion that relies on status or familiarity.
Protect personnel information and formal rating authority during comparison.
takeaways: Evidence comes before seniority or familiarity.
Formal authority and privacy remain intact.
lessons.statement: A responsible comparison asks how the judgment was reached, not how many people like the employee.

image.caption: Calibration can examine standards without becoming a popularity contest.

intro.heading: Make the reasoning available for examination
intro.body:
Supervisors may interpret the same standard differently. One may call a product satisfactory because it is accurate, while another expects additional analysis that was never explained. A responsible calibration discussion can examine these differences before a review is finalized. It should not become a vote about employees, a forced ranking invented by the course or a way for a senior person’s impression to override relevant evidence.

Follow the current agency process for who may participate, what information may be shared and who has formal rating authority. This lesson does not create a new review committee. When comparison is appropriate, bring the standard, relevant example, context and proposed reasoning. Limit information to what the authorized discussion needs and keep personnel records in approved channels.

Ask the same reasoning questions. Which expectation applies? What evidence demonstrates it? Was it explained and was the employee given an appropriate chance to respond? What condition affects interpretation? These questions help uncover hidden standards or uneven evidence without assigning motives to a supervisor. A disagreement is useful when it produces a clearer work basis.

Watch for status and familiarity shortcuts. “I know this person is excellent” needs relevant examples. “The director prefers this style” needs a work-related requirement, not an automatic override. An employee’s visibility to senior leaders may differ from the quality of their actual contribution. Compare what the role required and what the evidence supports.

If the discussion reveals a formal process question, seek HR guidance rather than making an improvised rule. Do not invent a rating distribution or adjust an individual’s rating solely to create an identity balance. Fairness requires relevant standards and lawful, appropriate procedures. Record the supported reasoning through the responsible process and identify any evidence that still needs examination.

lessons.keyStatement: Calibration examines the basis of a judgment; it does not replace formal authority with a group vote.

items.title: A senior leader remembers the employee
items.body: Memory and familiarity can suggest an example to examine, but they are not the standard. Ask which work evidence supports the claim. Do not disregard genuine expertise; make its relevance visible so another authorized reader can understand the reasoning.

items.title: The group wants equal numbers in each rating
items.body: This course does not authorize a rating distribution or forced comparison. Follow actual agency and employment procedures. If someone proposes a distribution, confirm its formal basis with HR rather than treating it as a convenient way to make the spreadsheet look balanced.

items.title: A discussion includes unnecessary personal information
items.body: Limit the material to the authorized review purpose and current handling rules. Private medical details or inferred cultural orientations do not belong in an informal calibration conversation. If sensitive information is relevant to a formal process, seek responsible guidance rather than improvising its use.

tabs.label: Standard
tabs.body: A standard identifies the actual requirement and whether it was communicated. An authorized comparison should not quietly repair a hidden expectation by applying it backward. Ask what the job required and how the employee could know it. This keeps attention on the basis of judgment rather than on a vote about who seems more impressive.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence includes relevant examples, context and limits. A senior supervisor may bring useful knowledge, but familiarity with an employee does not establish performance under a criterion. Ask what supports the judgment and consider contrary information appropriately. A review becomes more consistent by examining the same work question, not by requiring everyone to adopt the strongest voice’s impression.

tabs.label: Authority
tabs.body: Authority identifies who makes the formal judgment and how reasoning is recorded. A comparison meeting does not create unlimited power to adjust ratings or share private records. Keep discussion within approved participants and processes. If the evidence or procedure is uncertain, use responsible guidance rather than inventing a balancing adjustment based on identity or popularity.

check.question: During an authorized comparison, a senior supervisor says an employee deserves a high assessment because they are well known. What should the group ask?
check.correct: Which relevant work evidence and applicable standard support the judgment, including any important context or limits?
wrong: How many people in the room personally like the employee?
Which identity-based adjustment would make the chart look balanced?
check.feedbackCorrect: The question makes the judgment examinable without rejecting expertise or substituting popularity for the standard.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Popularity does not demonstrate performance under the relevant standard. An identity-based adjustment aimed solely at making a chart appear balanced bypasses the actual evidence. Seniority can bring knowledge but does not remove the need to explain it. Ask which work example, standard and context support the judgment within the authorized process.

items.text: The supervisor explains how the product met the stated accuracy requirement.
The director likes this employee, so no example is needed.
Confirm who is authorized to receive personnel information.
The group examines a dependency that affected the deadline.
Everyone recognizes the employee’s name, so the contribution must be stronger.
Seek HR guidance before introducing a new rating distribution.

lessons.next: Next, hold the review conversation with clear feedback and a chance to respond.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: In an authorized review discussion, Daniel supports a rating by saying that senior leaders often see Vera present. Another employee’s accurate research is less visible. The stated standard concerns the quality and usefulness of analysis, not presentation frequency.
options: Relevant analysis evidence and contribution against the standard, including visibility differences and appropriate records.
The number of senior leaders who recognize each employee.
An invented quota that determines ratings before the work is examined.
responses: This makes the judgment accountable to the standard rather than familiarity.
Recognition is not a substitute for the required work evidence.
An invented distribution does not establish an appropriate formal process.

lessons.transfer: Practice a practice calibration statement with standard, example, context and limit. Write two questions that examine the reasoning without labeling the supervisor’s motive.

move.control: You can explain your judgment and ask relevant questions within the authorized review process.
move.failure: A comparison meeting amplifies seniority and popularity while work standards become secondary.
move.next: Use a standard-and-evidence account in the next authorized review comparison.

lessons.title: Hold a clear conversation and invite a response
lessons.summary: Discuss evidence and next steps without avoiding difficult feedback or making identity the explanation.
lessons.objective: Structure a review conversation around expectation, evidence and employee response.
objectives: Structure a review conversation around expectation, evidence and employee response.
Write a constructive response to disagreement about an example.
Distinguish learning support from a formal employment or complaint process.
takeaways: Explain the basis before the conclusion.
A response can add relevant evidence.
Support and formal processes have distinct roles.
lessons.statement: A fair conversation allows the evidence to be examined while keeping responsibility for the work clear.

image.caption: The employee’s response can clarify evidence, context and next steps.

intro.heading: Discuss the work with clarity and respect
intro.body:
A supervisor may try to make a review comfortable by avoiding a real concern, or make it efficient by announcing a conclusion without inviting response. Neither approach gives the employee a useful account of the work. A clear conversation explains the expectation, relevant example, effect and next step, then provides an appropriate opportunity for the employee to respond through the responsible process.

Begin with the purpose and structure. Explain that the conversation will examine work evidence and priorities, not diagnose character or culture. Use specific examples and distinguish a supported finding from an open question. If formal procedures prescribe particular steps or documentation, follow them; this course does not replace those requirements.

Listen to the response for relevant evidence. The employee may identify a missing instruction, dependency or contribution the supervisor did not know about. Do not treat disagreement itself as disrespect. Check the new information and adjust the reasoning if warranted. At the same time, an employee’s disagreement does not automatically erase a supported concern or the supervisor’s responsibility to address it.

Agree on an actionable next step. What should the employee do differently, what support is appropriate and when will the result be reviewed? Keep the action proportionate to the work. Do not require a personal cultural explanation or completion of optional learning as a new formal condition without authority. Voluntary resources can be offered as support; actual performance actions follow current procedures.

If the employee raises a formal concern about discrimination, accommodation or another issue, explain and follow the responsible route. Do not use the performance conversation to adjudicate that concern informally or demand silence in exchange for a favorable review. Respectful treatment and credible procedures support clear accountability; they are not alternatives to it.

When a conversation raises an allegation or incident of protected-class harassment or discrimination, MMB Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report it immediately to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow current agency procedures. Do not wait for a learning agreement or use the performance discussion to investigate or determine the concern informally.

lessons.keyStatement: A response is evidence to examine, not a test of whether the employee accepts every impression without question.

items.title: The employee disagrees with the example
items.body: Ask which part is disputed and what relevant information is missing. Check the response through the appropriate process. A calm disagreement can improve accuracy. Avoid converting the act of questioning into a new personality concern unless separate evidence and applicable conduct requirements support it.

items.title: The supervisor wants to avoid discomfort
items.body: Respectful clarity is more useful than vague reassurance. State the work issue, effect and practical next step. Do not add unsupported personal labels or soften the message until the employee cannot understand it. Calling-in preserves dignity while addressing real responsibilities.

items.title: The employee raises a formal concern
items.body: Explain the designated route and follow duties that apply to your role. The review should not become an improvised investigation or a bargain about reporting. Appropriate practical support can continue while the formal issue is handled through its responsible process.

tabs.label: Explain
tabs.body: Explanation presents the expectation, evidence and work effect clearly enough to examine. Distinguish confirmed findings from open questions. An employee can respond more usefully to a concrete example than to a character label. Explaining the basis does not require abandoning accountability; it makes the relevant standard and reasoning visible.

tabs.label: Listen
tabs.body: Listening allows relevant new information to improve the account. If the employee identifies a missing dependency, check how it affected the task before confirming or revising the judgment. Respectful disagreement is not itself disloyalty or a developmental deficit. Neither dismiss the information because of status nor remove every expectation merely to end the conversation.

tabs.label: Agree
tabs.body: Agreement names the next work action, support and review point within actual authority. It need not imply agreement with every past interpretation. Keep optional learning separate from formal review requirements. If a concern involves protected-class harassment or discrimination, managers must immediately report it to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow current procedures.

check.question: An employee identifies a missing dependency in the supervisor’s review example. What is the strongest response?
check.correct: Examine the new information and its relevance to the standard before confirming or revising the judgment.
wrong: Treat the response as disloyalty because it questions the supervisor.
Automatically remove every expectation to avoid disagreement.
Ask the employee to explain their cultural background instead of the dependency.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response can improve the evidence while preserving accountability to the actual work standard.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling the response disloyalty suppresses potentially relevant evidence. Removing all expectations to avoid disagreement loses the work standard. Asking about cultural background ignores the actual dependency. Examine the new information and its effect, then confirm or revise the judgment through the appropriate process while preserving accountability.

items.text: Check the employee’s relevant evidence about the missing instruction.
Questioning an example proves the employee is disloyal.
Explain the designated route for an accommodation concern.
Agree on a specific revision and appropriate review point.
An unfamiliar accent explains poor commitment.
Follow applicable HR procedures for a formal employment action.

lessons.next: Next, review the performance process and improve its consistency.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: During a review, Alicia explains that a requested analysis changed after the deadline was agreed. Supervisor Grant did not know this and initially interprets her response as defensiveness. The change can be checked in the appropriate work records.
options: Add defensiveness as a new concern without examining the change.
Check the relevant information, explain its effect on the judgment and agree on a clear next step through the responsible process.
Require Alicia to attend optional learning before he will hear her response.
responses: This turns an evidence question into an unsupported personal label.
This makes the conversation accurate and actionable while retaining supervisory responsibility.
Optional learning should not become an unauthorized gate to a fair response.

lessons.transfer: Practice a practice review conversation with expectation, example, effect, employee response, revised reasoning if needed, and next action.

move.control: You can explain feedback, examine a response and agree on support while preserving formal responsibilities.
move.failure: The employee learns that raising relevant evidence is treated as a character problem.
move.next: Prepare two evidence questions and a clear next-step statement for the next review conversation.

lessons.title: Review consistency without profiling employees
lessons.summary: Examine the review process, evidence and support over time while protecting personnel information.
lessons.objective: Select a process question for improving review consistency.
objectives: Select a process question for improving review consistency.
Identify a comparison that requires more context or responsible data guidance.
Develop one improvement with an owner and a practical result check.
takeaways: Review the process as well as the result.
Improve consistency without personal cultural scores.
lessons.statement: A pattern in reviews should lead to an evidence-based process inquiry, not a hidden label attached to employees.

image.caption: Process review can improve clarity, evidence and feedback.

intro.heading: Improve the arrangements that produce the review
intro.body:
Leaders can examine whether reviews are clear and consistent without creating a new personnel profiling system. A useful inquiry asks about expectations, evidence coverage, wording, authorized comparison and follow-through. It does not infer an employee’s intercultural orientation from a rating or assume that a difference across groups has one cause. The purpose is to strengthen the process that produces work judgments.

Choose a specific question. Were important expectations explained before the review? Did significant judgments include relevant examples? Were employees offered an appropriate response? Did agreed support and follow-up occur? These process questions can reveal a practical improvement even when broad rating comparisons are not appropriate or information is limited.

If analyzing ratings or workforce patterns is authorized, use responsible definitions and data handling. Roles, periods, standards and assignment opportunities may differ. Small or distinctive populations may be identifiable despite omitted names. Seek HR and data practices guidance before reporting, and do not invent a minimum threshold or retention period for actual records.

Describe limits honestly. Missing evidence should not be shown as a reassuring empty chart. A rating difference can justify further inquiry, but it does not diagnose the cause or prove every individual judgment wrong. Likewise, similar ratings do not prove that expectations and support were fair. Review actual process evidence and appropriate accounts of experience.

Choose one improvement within authority. It might be clarifying a recurring vague expectation, giving a better work example, checking evidence across the period or explaining the response route. Name an owner and a result check. Consultant guidance can support thoughtful analysis while supervisors retain responsibility for their work and HR retains formal authority. A more dependable process develops through evidence and follow-through, not an unsupported claim that bias has been eliminated.

inThisLesson: Assign an improvement and result check.
lessons.keyStatement: Examine how judgments are made and supported without assigning hidden developmental or identity-based labels.

items.title: Ratings differ across role groups
items.body: The difference may reflect standards, assignments, evidence, decisions or other factors. Confirm comparable definitions and responsible data handling before interpreting it. Do not infer a single cause from a chart or change individual ratings solely to make group averages match.

items.title: Ratings look similar
items.body: Similar results do not establish that expectations, support and response opportunities were equally clear. Examine the process evidence. A review system can produce similar numbers while still leaving important work or contribution invisible. Avoid claiming success from one convenient measure.

items.title: Optional learning becomes an employee score
items.body: Course participation is not a licensed IDI result, commitment measure or hidden personnel label. Do not attach an inferred orientation to an employee or make voluntary learning an unauthorized access gate. Formal performance evidence and records remain within their approved procedures.

tabs.label: Finding
tabs.body: A finding describes the observed process gap and its evidence limits. An authorized report may show rating differences across groups, but not why they occurred. Check definitions, role mix, opportunities and privacy before interpreting the pattern. Individual assessment labels should not be invented from a chart or course response.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: An action responds to a supported arrangement, such as clarifying expectations earlier or reviewing access to relevant work. Obtain any required HR guidance and preserve formal authority. Automatically adjusting every rating to force identical averages does not examine whether the standards and evidence were appropriate. The improvement should address the process the evidence actually identifies.

tabs.label: Check
tabs.body: A check asks whether the next review uses clearer expectations and more relevant evidence. Record it through the approved process without creating a separate informal personnel score. A useful future change does not by itself settle an actual past concern. Keep that concern in its responsible route and review the improvement’s effects honestly.

check.question: A leader sees a rating difference across groups in an authorized report. What is the responsible next step?
check.correct: Check definitions, roles, opportunity and privacy limits, then examine process evidence before drawing an explanation or choosing a change.
wrong: Infer each employee’s developmental orientation from the rating.
Adjust ratings solely to make every group average identical.
Declare that the chart proves one cause without further evidence.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps the finding connected to a responsible inquiry and avoids overclaiming or personal profiling.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A rating cannot reveal an individual’s intercultural-development orientation. Making group averages identical without examining evidence can create unsupported individual adjustments. A chart alone cannot establish one cause. Check definitions, roles, opportunity and privacy, then examine responsible process evidence before selecting an improvement or drawing a conclusion.

items.text: Examine whether expectations were communicated before the review.
Matching averages proves bias has disappeared.
Replace a recurring vague phrase with a work-related example.
Check roles and periods before comparing authorized results.
A voluntary course score reveals the employee’s cultural stage.
Add an appropriate evidence-and-response check through the current review process.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare a clear, evidence-based and constructive review.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Omari notices several review drafts use “presence” without examples. He proposes a new employee potential dashboard. HR confirms that the immediate process question is how supervisors explain work expectations and evidence, not a new hidden score.
scenario.prompt: Which action best fits the finding?
options: Build the potential dashboard from optional course attendance.
Declare every existing review invalid without examining it.
Clarify the recurring expectation with relevant examples, support supervisors in applying it and check the next drafts through the responsible process.
responses: Attendance does not establish potential or developmental orientation and should not become a hidden personnel label.
The finding supports examination and correction, not an unsupported blanket conclusion.
This improves the process supported by the evidence while preserving formal authority and records.

lessons.transfer: Build a practice review-quality plan with one expectation gap, appropriate evidence, wording revision, response route, owner and result check.

move.control: You can improve clarity and evidence in responsible review processes without creating an informal profiling system.
move.failure: A fairness initiative produces hidden personal scores instead of clearer work judgments.
move.next: Select one recurring review-process gap and implement an authorized improvement with a concrete check.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare a review that explains its evidence and useful next steps.
remember: Explain the work standard before judging against it.
Separate observation, context and unsupported interpretation.
Protect formal processes and employee information.

sections.heading: Prepare
items: Connect expectations to the actual role and purpose.
Clarify significant changes prospectively through responsible procedures.
Gather relevant evidence across the period and responsibilities.
Examine access, dependencies and contrary evidence without erasing standards.

sections.heading: Write and compare
items: Use observation, work effect and practical next step.
Check whether style or familiarity is replacing capability evidence.
Compare reasoning only through authorized processes and participants.
Keep rating authority, applicable agreements and personnel records intact.

sections.heading: Converse and improve
items: Explain the basis and invite a relevant employee response.
Check new information and adjust reasoning where warranted.
Separate optional support from formal employment or complaint procedures.
Choose one process improvement with an owner and result check.
Never infer or record an individual IDI orientation from course activity or performance judgments.
